title: From Contact Maps to Causal Biology: Benchmarking and Validating Computational Methods for 3D Genome Interpretation
content: Background: The three-dimensional (3D) organization of the genome is a key factor in gene regulation, cellular differentiation and disease pathogenesis. Chromatin interaction studies have been revolutionized by the advent of high-throughput chromosome conformation capture technologies, such as Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, HiChIP, and single-cell Hi-C. However, computational analysis of these data remains challenging. This review aims to critically evaluate computational methods for 3D genome interpretation, with an emphasis on benchmarking strategies, methodological limitations and the experimental evidence supporting computational predictions. Methods: We performed targeted searches of PubMed and Google Scholar databases for studies published between January 2015 and August 2026 and followed up with reference chaining to find peer-reviewed publications related to computational analysis, benchmarking and experimental validation in 3D genomics. The emphasis is on representative and influential methods, not an exhaustive list. The cited evidence base excluded preprints, theses, duplicate citations or non-peer reviewed materials. Results: The literature can be divided into six recurring themes: TAD detection, loop calling, A/B compartment analysis, 3D structure reconstruction, deep learning, and single-cell Hi-C analysis. In all these divisions, we found that the reported performance is highly sensitive to sequencing depth, matrix resolution, assay type, cell type, preprocessing, and the selection of the validation proxy. Due to the lack of a universal biological ground truth, studies often integrate simulations, cross-method agreements, protein or histone enrichment, orthogonal assays, imaging, and perturbation experiments. Conclusions: Methodologically, the study of the 3D genome by computation is very diverse and is dependent on the study design. Transparent reporting, depth- and resolution-aware evaluation, orthogonal validation, and explicit separation of predictive accuracy from biological causality are essential for reliable interpretation. Future studies should focus on reproducible benchmark datasets, cross-assay testing, interpretable models, and experimentally testable chromatin structure-to-function relationships.
